items.t: Inside the Codex sandbox
items.x: See how Codex runs commands on your machine while enforcing the filesystem and network limits you control across macOS, Linux, and Windows.
items.xd:
SpaceXSI (formerly xAI) is not involved in this article; it covers OpenAI's Codex sandbox. Here is a plain-language summary.

OpenAI describes a "defense in depth" approach to keeping AI agents safe. Along with training and alignment, it adds protections to Codex, its agent tool. One key protection is the Codex sandbox, which lets Codex run commands on a user's computer while staying within filesystem and network limits the user sets.

A sandbox limits what a program can access while it runs. For example, a user organizing photos could let Codex change files only in their Pictures folder and block network access so nothing gets uploaded. For code review, a user could allow access to online documentation while keeping source files read-only. Users set these rules through permission profiles, which define the filesystem and network restrictions for a Codex session.

Codex's default settings are meant to be cautious but still useful. With a Git repository as the workspace, the built-in workspace profile allows writing inside the workspace while keeping folders such as .git and .codex read-only. This stops direct changes to config files and Git hooks, so Codex can edit source code without asking permission for every change.

The default profile also allows broad reading of files across the computer, because build tools need libraries and settings stored outside the project. The tradeoff is that sensitive files elsewhere, such as config files containing API keys, may still be readable. Network access is disabled by default, which blocks uploads to outside services and also blocks legitimate actions like downloading dependencies.

The article notes that these limits do not stop every harmful action. For instance, the agent could inject malicious code into a locally installed package that isn't tracked by Git, and that code could run later outside the sandbox. This is why OpenAI combines the sandbox with training and alignment.

Unlike many tools that isolate work in a virtual machine or container, Codex uses each operating system's own sandboxing features to constrain commands in the user's existing environment. OpenAI says this keeps things simpler, since many developers' tools, such as an iOS build toolchain on a Mac, cannot run inside a container.

Codex exposes this sandboxing through a common API across macOS, Windows, and Linux. When a command runs, the harness starts it in a sandbox using the chosen permission profile and, if network access is limited, a network proxy. Child processes inherit the same restrictions. When a command needs more access than the default allows, the harness decides whether to grant it, based on user preferences, by prompting the user or routing the request to auto-review.

Users can define their own profiles in a configuration file. The article gives an example profile called dev that extends the built-in workspace profile, adds write access to a build cache folder, and makes a .vscode folder read-only. Filesystem entries can be read-only, read-write, or blocked. Network access can be fully enabled, or restricted to specific domains, with explicit deny rules taking precedence over allow rules.

Individual users can set defaults and override them for trusted projects. Enterprise administrators can set defaults for their users and limit which profiles those users can choose, using layered configuration and managed requirements files.

The codex sandbox command lets people test a profile by running any command under it, to confirm the sandbox blocks what it should. For example, a test attempting to write a malicious auto-formatter into a read-only .vscode folder should be blocked. The same sandboxing can also be used by developers in their own tools.

Codex does not sandbox the command that starts a stdio MCP server, because it cannot reliably know what files or network services that server needs. The article gives an example where the memory MCP server is wrapped in a custom profile that limits writes to its cache and data folders and blocks network access. The package is pre-cached so the server can start offline.

On the technical side, the network proxy handles requests and checks them against domain rules. It resolves a hostname only after confirming the request is allowed or approved, to avoid leaking information through DNS. On macOS, Codex uses Apple's Seatbelt, which is kernel-enforced, through a policy language that is not documented for third-party use. On Linux, Codex uses bubblewrap to build an isolated filesystem view and network namespace, plus seccomp-bpf filters to restrict system calls. On Windows, Codex previously built its own sandbox and is now transitioning to a sandbox based on Microsoft's MXC library, which supports containment on Windows, Linux, and macOS.

items.t: NVIDIA Announces Rubin HPC — A New GPU to Accelerate Agents for Science, Engineering and Analytics
items.x: Announced today at SC26, NVIDIA Rubin HPC is a new GPU in the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform designed to accelerate simulation and data processing for science, engineering and analytics workflows. As agents help scientists and engineers explore more candidate materials, molecules and designs, they rely on simulations to test those ideas and guide their next […]
items.xd:
NVIDIA announced Rubin HPC at the SC26 conference today. It is a new GPU in the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform, built to speed up simulation and data processing for science, engineering and analytics work.

AI agents are helping scientists and engineers explore more candidate materials, molecules and designs. To test those ideas and decide on next steps, they need simulations, and Rubin HPC is meant to make those simulations faster. This shortens the path from exploration to scientific discovery and industrial design.

The Rubin HPC GPU has a record number of CUDA cores, more than 50,000 on a single chip. It also includes a sparse data acceleration capability that keeps those cores supplied with data, and it speeds up connections between GPUs using seventh-generation NVIDIA NVLink interconnect technology.

Scientists and engineers use simulation to understand complex systems before running experiments or building physical prototypes. Working with agents, they can review more options, which increases the need for the GPU-accelerated simulations that evaluate those options.

Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA, said that faster simulation means faster discovery for agents working on science and engineering. He said Rubin HPC helps scientists and engineers explore more possibilities and brings breakthroughs closer.

Many fields, including climate modeling, engineering, genomic analysis and financial risk, share a similar computing pattern. An application pulls a few scattered values from a huge dataset, performs a calculation, and repeats this at very large scale.

To address this, Rubin HPC uses a balanced design that scales data movement and compute together, instead of increasing compute alone. This keeps its many CUDA cores fed with data so they spend more time computing and less time waiting. It speeds up common patterns in simulation work, including sparse matrix operations, stencil computations, sorting and reductions.

These patterns appear across data analytics, science and engineering, so a purpose-built GPU offering broad acceleration can help drive breakthroughs in many industries.

NVIDIA's CUDA-X libraries provide a growing set of optimized versions of complex algorithms for agents to use, especially those relevant to simulation and analytics. Used with Rubin HPC, these libraries can help agents reach reasoning results faster.

Faster simulations also give quicker feedback, which shortens the cycle of forming a hypothesis, simulating it and refining it. This lets researchers and engineers choose next steps sooner and focus lab work on the most promising candidates.

Rubin HPC is expected to be available in 2028.

items.t: Advancing computer-use agents for healthcare teams
items.x: Healthcare information is often scattered across many systems, so staff must move it by hand before a patient can get care.
items.xd:
Healthcare information is often scattered across many systems, so staff must move it by hand before a patient can get care. For example, a clinician may order an MRI, but the insurer needs details stored in the patient's record, and someone has to pull them out and enter them into a separate portal to finish an authorization request.

Computer-use agents complete multi-step tasks by clicking, typing, and switching between programs. In healthcare, this lets AI handle repetitive jobs inside the software teams already rely on.

OpenAI is sharing new results on how well these models perform, how safe they are, and what they cost in clinical and administrative work. It is also working with healthcare organizations including Abridge, Ambience, Cigna Healthcare, and CVS Health on computer use for authorization requests, referrals, discharge planning, and outreach between visits.

Healthcare teams, developers, and individual clinicians can use these features now through the OpenAI API, ChatGPT for Healthcare, and ChatGPT for Clinicians. Organizations can run HIPAA-compliant workflows, set approvals and agent access, and keep audit logs for secure deployments.

To show how an agent could help a clinician and an authorization specialist handle the same MRI request, OpenAI built a demo with synthetic patient data. In it, a patient messages their clinician about lower back pain, and the agent reviews the visit notes, physical therapy records, and earlier imaging in the EHR. It then drafts an MRI order, an encounter note, and a patient reply for the clinician to check. Using the same records, the agent prepares a prior authorization request in the insurer's portal for a specialist to review.

OpenAI tested GPT‑6 Astra on tasks clinicians handle in their EHR inboxes, which physicians helped shape. These tasks required multi-step work that tested both clinical reasoning across a patient's history and navigation of complicated interfaces. Reviewers looked at the model's actions along with the notes, orders, and messages it produced, judging whether the work would be helpful and clinically safe.

Reviewers judged whether errors, gaps, or actions could plausibly harm a patient. Of 325 tasks reviewed, 99% were rated safe. Physicians rated helpfulness on a five-point scale, choosing "very helpful" or "extremely helpful" in 93% of 646 assessments.

OpenAI also tested computer-use agents on administrative jobs such as prior authorizations, appeals, and medical equipment orders. On HealthAdminBench, an independent benchmark from Stanford researchers that measures common administrative workflows, GPT‑6 Astra earned 94.3% of the available rubric points. GPT‑6 Luna earned 91.8% while costing 98% less, at 8.5 cents per task. Both models ran at maximum reasoning effort. OpenAI says these results show progress toward capable, affordable agents for high-volume administrative work.

CVS Health uses OpenAI's computer-use capabilities to automate repeated work across clinical systems, including sending documents, processing referrals, and supporting specialist consults. The agents work inside existing applications to finish steps that APIs do not fully cover. In one production workflow, an agent cleared a backlog of document sends that had built up over months, doing it over a single weekend. Another agent handles the system steps for tens of thousands of consults each day, so staff can focus on work that needs their expertise. CVS Health uses validation checks, human oversight, and screenshots and action records to verify what the agents did. It is open sourcing its Agent Kit, built with OpenAI's Agents SDK, as a repeatable approach for wider use.

CVS Health keeps its data inside its enterprise-controlled infrastructure, under its enterprise AI Governance team and responsible AI policies. Production data is not used to train foundation models.

Abridge is building computer-use agents that help clinicians carry out care plans in the apps they use every day, including ones without APIs. Its planned inpatient use case starts from the clinical conversation and adds EHR information and nurse and clinician context to flag what needs attention and coordinate next steps. A clinician might ask the Abridge Assistant to clear a patient's discharge barriers, and agents could work at the same time on medication access and home-health coordination, using computer interaction along with calls and messages. The clinician stays focused on the patient and steps in for decisions that need clinical judgment.

As part of The Cigna Group's wider collaboration with OpenAI, Cigna Healthcare uses OpenAI's frontier models with its own clinical expertise to pull relevant information from many systems and give care teams a fuller picture of each member's needs. That can include benefits and coverage, providers, appointments, and past interactions, helping teams support care plans set by treating providers. Cigna Healthcare case managers previously had to move through more than 10 separate clinical and administrative systems to gather this context. Computer use can now navigate those systems and combine the relevant information in seconds, cutting search time and giving case managers more time with members.

Computer use lets agents complete tasks in EHRs and payer portals that APIs cannot reach. In healthcare, that only works if every action can be controlled and audited, so Ambience built extra controls for oversight. In its demonstration, Ambience uses evidence from the patient's chart to prepare a prior-authorization request on an insurer's website. When the record is unclear, the agent stops to ask the clinician and waits for approval before submitting. Health systems decide which actions the agent may take, can pause it at any time, and receive a step-by-step log for audits.

Healthcare startups are turning advances in computer use into new ways to support care teams. Five companies are pairing AI agents with healthcare expertise to help teams navigate systems, coordinate next steps, and keep care moving.

Computer-use agents in healthcare call for evaluating clinical safety, protecting patient information, and setting clear limits on what agents can do without human review.

ChatGPT for Healthcare offers role-based access controls and audit logs for oversight. Organizations can add their own review and approval steps and configure the applications and environments agents use, limiting access to the records and actions each task needs. Organization data is not used to train OpenAI foundation models.

For HIPAA-compliant workflows involving protected health information, organizations must use eligible services covered by their Business Associate Agreement with OpenAI, along with the required security and retention settings.

Computer-use agents for healthcare are available now in ChatGPT for Healthcare, ChatGPT for Clinicians, and the OpenAI API. Healthcare organizations can contact OpenAI's sales team to discuss AI for clinical and administrative workflows, and existing customers can ask their workspace administrator to enable computer use in ChatGPT Work and Codex. U.S. clinicians can sign up for a free ChatGPT for Clinicians account and try computer use in ChatGPT Work and Codex. Developers can build healthcare applications with the OpenAI API and follow the computer use guide to create agents that work across existing software.

OpenAI hopes these advances let healthcare teams spend less time moving information between systems and more time caring for patients.
